''' Yasunobu Nakamura '''(中村 泰信 '''Nakamura Yasunobu''') is a Japanese [[physicist]]. He is a professor at the [[University of Tokyo]]'s Research Center for Advanced Science and Technology (RCAST)<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ap.t.u-tokyo.ac.jp/en/research.html |title=Research Groups |access-date=2016-12-21}}</ref> and the Principal Investigator of the Superconducting Quantum Electronics Research Group (SQERG) at the Center for Emergent Matter Science (CEMS) within [[RIKEN]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.riken.jp/en/research/labs/cems/superconduct_qtm_electron/ |title=Superconducting Quantum Electronics Research Group |access-date=2020-10-22}}</ref> He has contributed primarily to the area of [[quantum information science]],<ref>T. D. Ladd, F. Jelezko, R. Laflamme, Y. Nakamura, C. Monroe, and J.L. O'Brien, "Quantum computers", ''Nature'' '''464''', 45-53 (2010), {{doi|10.1038/nature08812}}, [https://arxiv.org/abs/1009.2267 arxiv:1009:2267]</ref> particularly in [[superconducting quantum computing]] and hybrid quantum systems.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://news.mynavi.jp/news/2015/07/10/500/ |title=マイナビニュース |date=2015-07-10 |access-date=2016-12-22}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ryosi.com/qis/201611/01/ |title=ようこそ量子 Interview |date=2016-11-15 |access-date=2016-12-22}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2015/08/150803105119.htm |title=Science Daily 2015 |date=2015-08-03 |access-date=2016-12-22}}</ref>

== Education and early work ==
While a child, Nakamura's family moved from [[Osaka, Japan|Osaka]] to [[Hinode, Tokyo]], where he would gain his early education.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.u-tokyo.ac.jp/focus/en/features/voices066.html |title=UTokyo Voices 066 |date=2019-06-20 |access-date=2019-06-21}}</ref> He obtained his [[Bachelor of Science]] (1990), [[Master of Science]] (1992), and [[Ph.D.]] (2011) degrees at the [[University of Tokyo]]. In 1999, as a researcher at [[NEC]], Nakamura and collaborators Yuri Pashkin and [[Jaw-Shen Tsai]] demonstrated "electrical coherent control of a qubit in a solid-state electronic device"<ref name="Nature1999" /> and in 2001 "realized the first measurement of the Rabi oscillations associated with the transition between two [[Josephson effect|Josephson]] levels in the [[Cooper pair box]]"<ref name="BellPrize2013">{{cite web |url=http://cqiqc.physics.utoronto.ca/bell_prize/devoret_schoelkopf.html |title=Bell Prize 2013 |access-date=2016-12-21 |archive-date=2014-06-04 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140604060818/http://cqiqc.physics.utoronto.ca/bell_prize/devoret_schoelkopf.html |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>Y. Nakamura, Y.A. Pashkin, and J.S. Tsai, "Rabi Oscillations in a Josephson-Junction Charge Two-Level System", ''Physical Review Letters'' '''87''', 246601 (2001), {{doi|10.1103/PhysRevLett.87.246601}}</ref> in a configuration developed by [[Michel Devoret]] and colleagues in 1998.<ref name="BellPrize2013" /><ref>V. Bouchiat, D. Vion, P. Joyez, D. Esteve and M. H. Devoret, "Quantum coherence with a single Cooper pair", ''[[Physica Scripta]]'' '''T76''', 165-170 (1998), {{doi|10.1238/Physica.Topical.076a00165}}</ref>

In 2000, Nakamura was featured as a "Younger Scientist" by the [[Japan Society of Applied Physics]] for his work at [[NEC]] in "quantum-state control of nanoscale superconducting devices."<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.jsap.or.jp/jsapi/Pdf/Number02/YoungerScientists.pdf |title=JSAP Younger Scientists |access-date=2016-12-21}}</ref> From 2001-2002, he visited the group of {{ill|Hans Mooij|de}} at [[TU Delft]] on a sabbatical from NEC, where he worked with Irinel Chiorescu, Kees Harmans, and Mooij to create the first [[flux qubit]].<ref>I. Chiorescu, Y. Nakamura, C. J. P. M. Harmans, and J. E. Mooij, "Coherent Quantum Dynamics of a Superconducting Flux Qubit", ''Science'' '''299''', 5614, 1869-1871, (2003), {{doi|10.1126/science.1081045}}, [https://arxiv.org/abs/cond-mat/0305461 arxiv:0305461]</ref><ref>J. Clarke, "Flux Qubit Completes the Hat Trick", ''Science'' '''299''', 5614, 1850-1851, (2003),
 {{doi|10.1126/science.1083001}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://blog.qutech.nl/index.php/2017/11/04/the-first-delft-qubit/ |title=The first Delft qubit |work=QuTech Blog |date=2017-11-04 |access-date=2017-11-04}}</ref> In 2003, he was named one of [[MIT Technology Review]]'s top innovators under 35 years old, in which editors noted that "Nakamura and a collaborator got two [[qubits]] to interact in a manner that had been predicted but never demonstrated" at the time.<ref name="TechReviewUnder35">{{cite web |url=http://www2.technologyreview.com/tr35/profile.aspx?TRID=414 |title=Innovators Under 35 |work=MIT Technology Review |access-date=2016-12-21 |archive-date=2016-07-01 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160701044937/http://www2.technologyreview.com/tr35/profile.aspx?trid=414 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

== Current work ==
{{As of|2016|10|03}}, the Japan Science and Technology Agency (科学技術振興機構) announced funding for Nakamura's work through their Exploratory Research for Advanced Technology (ERATO) program.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.jst.go.jp/pr/info/info1218/index.html |title=戦略的創造研究推進事業における |access-date=2016-12-21 |archive-date=2016-12-25 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161225180242/http://www.jst.go.jp/pr/info/info1218/index.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> The project, entitled Macroscopic Quantum Machines,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.jst.go.jp/pr/info/info1218/shiryou1.html |title=研究総括および研究領域 |access-date=2016-12-21}}</ref> seeks to dramatically improve quantum state control technology to further the field of [[quantum computing]]. Of principal focus is the development of a highly scalable platform for implementing quantum information processing techniques, as well as the creation of hybrid quantum systems which interface with microwave [[quantum optics]]. In an article in {{ill|Nikkei Science|ja|日経サイエンス}} in 2018, it was announced that work towards the construction of a quantum computer with 100 [[superconducting qubits]] was underway.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nikkei-science.com/201809_008.html |title=超電導量子ビットを創始 100ビットを目指す |date=September 2018 |access-date=2019-06-21}}</ref> In 2019, the Japanese [[Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology]] launched a quantum technology project known as QLEAP, with Nakamura as the team leader for the quantum information processing component.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.jst.go.jp/stpp/q-leap/index.html |title=光・量子飛躍フラッグシッププログラム（Q-LEAP） |access-date=2019-04-03}}</ref> The project aims to develop superconducting quantum computers and other quantum technologies over a ten-year period, by increasing collaboration between academia and industry.

[[File:Impedence-Matched Lambda-type Three-Level System, 10.1038.ncomms12303 (Inomata et al., 2016).png|thumb|A [[flux qubit]] and [[superconducting]] [[microwave cavity]] form a [[coupling (physics)|coupled]] system that connects to a [[parametric oscillator|parametric phase-locked oscillator]]. In the paper [https://www.nature.com/articles/ncomms12303 "Single microwave-photon detector using an artificial Λ-type three-level system"] published in [[Nature Communications]] in 2016, Nakamura and collaborators manipulated this three-level system in such a way that single photons were detected with an "efficiency of 0.66±0.06 with a low [[Single-photon avalanche diode#Internal noise and afterpulsing|dark-count]] probability of 0.014±0.001 and a reset time of ~400 ns."<ref name="NatureCommunications2016">K. Inomata, Z. Lin, K. Koshino, W. D. Oliver, J.- S. Tsai, T. Yamamoto, and Y. Nakamura, "Single microwave-photon detector using an artificial Λ-type three-level system", ''[[Nature Communications]]'' '''7''', 12303 (2016), {{doi|10.1038/ncomms12303|doi-access=free}}</ref>]] In past years, Nakamura and collaborators have published their findings on the efficient detection of single [[microwave]] frequency [[photons]],<ref name="NatureCommunications2016" /> the suppression of [[quasiparticles]] in superconducting quantum computing environments for the improvement of qubit [[Coherence (physics)|coherence]] [[Relaxation (NMR)#T1 and T2|times]],<ref name="Science2016">S. Gustavsson, F. Yan, G. Catelani, J. Bylander, A. Kamal, J. Birenbaum, D. Hover, D. Rosenberg, G. Samach, A. P. Sears, S. J. Weber, J. L. Yoder, J. Clarke, A. J. Kerman, F. Yoshihara, Y. Nakamura, T. P. Orlando, and W. D. Oliver, "Suppressing relaxation in superconducting qubits by quasiparticle pumping", ''Science'' '''354''', 6319, 1573-1577 (2016), {{doi|10.1126/science.aah5844}}</ref> the development of "a deterministic scheme to generate maximal [[Quantum entanglement|entanglement]] between remote superconducting atoms, using a propagating microwave photon as a flying qubit",<ref>K. Koshino, K. Inomata, Z. R. Lin, Y. Tokunaga, T. Yamamoto, and Y. Nakamura, "Theory of Deterministic Entanglement Generation between Remote Superconducting Atoms", ''[[Physical Review Applied]]'' '''7''', 064006 (2017), {{doi|10.1103/PhysRevApplied.7.064006}}</ref> and the realization of a hybrid quantum system by the strong, [[coherence (physics)|coherent]] [[Coupling (physics)#Quantum mechanics|coupling]] between a collective magnetic [[Normal mode#Mode|mode]] of a [[ferromagnetic]] sphere and a superconducting qubit.<ref name="Science2015" />

More recently, results have been published in which superconducting qubits were used to resolve quanta of [[magnon]] number states,<ref>D. Lachance-Quiriom, Y. Tabuchi, S. Ishino, A. Noguchi, T. Ishikawa, R. Yamazaki, and Y. Nakamura, "Resolving quanta of collective spin excitations in a millimeter-sized ferromagnet", ''[[Science Advances]]'' '''3''', ''7'', e1603150 (2017), {{doi|10.1126/sciadv.1603150}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.u-tokyo.ac.jp/focus/en/articles/a_00582.html |title=Quantifying quanta |date=2017-11-22 |access-date=2019-04-03}}</ref> to create a quantitatively non-classical photon number distribution,<ref>S. Kono, Y. Masuyama, T. Ishikawa, Y. Tabuchi, R. Yamazaki, K. Usami, K. Koshino, and Y. Nakamura, "Nonclassical Photon Number Distribution in a Superconducting Cavity under a Squeezed Drive", ''[[Physical Review Letters]]'' '''119''', 023602 (2017), {{doi|10.1103/PhysRevLett.119.023602}}</ref>  to measure fluctuations in a [[surface acoustic wave]] (SAW) resonator,<ref>A. Noguchi, R. Yamazaki, Y. Tabuchi, and Y. Nakamura, "Qubit-Assisted Transduction for a Detection of Surface Acoustic Waves near the Quantum Limit", ''[[Physical Review Letters]]'' '''119''', 180505 (2017), {{doi|10.1103/PhysRevLett.119.180505}}</ref> and to measure an itinerant microwave photon in a [[quantum nondemolition]] (QND) detection experiment.<ref>S. Kono, K. Koshino, Y. Tabuchi, A. Noguchi, and Y. Nakamura, "Quantum non-demolition detection of an itinerant microwave photon", ''[[Nature Physics]]'' '''14''', 546-549 (2018), {{doi|10.1038/s41567-018-0066-3}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|url=https://physics.aps.org/articles/v11/38 |title=Viewpoint: Single Microwave Photons Spotted on the Rebound |journal=Physics |date=2018-04-23 |volume=11 |page=38 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevX.8.021003 |access-date=2019-04-03 |last1=Murch |first1=Kater W. |arxiv=1711.11569 }}</ref> A superconducting circuit was later used to realize information-to-work conversion by a [[Maxwell's demon]],<ref>Y. Masuyama, K. Funo, Y. Murashita, A. Noguchi, S. Kono, Y. Tabuchi, R. Yamazaki, M. Ueda, and Y. Nakamura, "Information-to-work conversion by Maxwell’s demon in a superconducting circuit quantum electrodynamical system", ''[[Nature Communications]]'' '''9''', 1291 (2018), {{doi|10.1038/s41467-018-03686-y|doi-access=free}}</ref> [[Radio-frequency engineering|radio waves]] and optical light were [[Cavity optomechanics|optomechanically]] coupled to surface acoustic waves,<ref>A. Okada, F. Oguro, A. Noguchi, Y. Tabuchi, R. Yamazaki, K. Usami, and Y. Nakamura, "Cavity Enhancement of Anti-Stokes Scattering via Optomechanical Coupling with Surface Acoustic Waves", ''[[Physical Review Applied]]'' '''10''', 024002 (2018), {{doi|10.1103/PhysRevApplied.10.024002}}</ref> and an ordered [[Topological defect|vortex]] lattice in a [[Josephson junction]] array was observed.<ref>R. Cosmic, K. Ikegami, Z. Lin, K. Inomata, J. M. Taylor, and Y. Nakamura, "Circuit-QED-based measurement of vortex lattice order in a Josephson junction array", ''[[Physical Review B]]'' '''98''', 060501(R) (2018), {{doi|10.1103/PhysRevB.98.060501}}</ref>

Nakamura has spoken several times at quantum information science conferences and seminars, including at the [[University of Vienna]],<ref>{{cite web |url=https://physik.univie.ac.at/en/wpk/wpk-detail/archive/2014/june//article/yasunobu-nakamura-research-center-for-advanced-science-and-technology-the-university-of-tokyo/?tx_ttnews%5BbackPid%5D=146952&cHash=133067e9dc3db92ea3243fede2bb6e1c |title=University of Vienna 2014 |access-date=2016-12-21 }}{{Dead link|date=July 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> the Institute for Theoretical Atomic Molecular and Optical Physics at [[Harvard University]],<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cfa.harvard.edu/itamp/LightMatterInteractionsinLowDimensions-schedule.html |title=ITAMP |access-date=2016-12-21}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CrjkLcimTX4 |title=ITAMP Video |website=[[YouTube]] |date=2015-07-15 |access-date=2016-12-22}}</ref> the National Center of Competence in Research's Quantum Science and Technology [[Monte Verità]] conference,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nccr-qsit.ethz.ch/news/conferences-events/monte-verita-2015/invited-speakers.html |title=NCCR QSIT |access-date=2016-12-21}}</ref> the [[Institute for Quantum Computing]] at the [[University of Waterloo]],<ref>{{cite web|url=https://uwaterloo.ca/institute-for-quantum-computing/events/seminar-yasunobu-nakamura |title=IQC 2016 |access-date=2016-12-21}}</ref> the [[Institute for Molecular Engineering]] at the [[University of Chicago]]<ref>{{cite web |url=https://ime.uchicago.edu/events/4549/ |title=IME Distinguished Colloquium Series |access-date=2019-04-03 |archive-date=2019-04-03 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190403070348/https://ime.uchicago.edu/events/4549/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> the [[Institute for Quantum Optics and Quantum Information]] (IQOQI),<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.iqoqi.at/en/current/gallery/2018/03102018-6th-iqoqi-colloquium-yasunobu-nakamura |title=IQOQI Colloquium |access-date=2019-04-03 |archive-date=2019-04-03 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190403070345/https://www.iqoqi.at/en/current/gallery/2018/03102018-6th-iqoqi-colloquium-yasunobu-nakamura |url-status=dead }}</ref> and the Yale Quantum Institute at [[Yale University]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://quantuminstitute.yale.edu/event/yqi-colloquium-yasunobu-nakamura-university-tokyo |title=YQI Colloquium |access-date=2019-04-03}}</ref>

In 2020, Nakamura was named as a fellow of the [[American Physical Society]] for "the first demonstration of coherent time-dependent manipulation of superconducting qubits, and for contributions to the development of superconducting quantum circuits, microwave quantum optics, and hybrid quantum systems".<ref name="APS2020">{{cite web|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm?initial=N |title=APS Fellows |access-date=2020-12-01}}</ref>
